In this masterful history, Douglas chronicles the long struggle to hold states to account for war crimes. He tells the dramatic story of the twentieth-century jurists, thinkers, and activists who redefined the norms of international law and justice, and inspired a worldwide movement to check the impunity of states. At the end of the nineteenth century, no rules constrained when states could engage in war. Douglas argues that an initial breakthrough occurred after World War I, when the victors sought to put the German kaiser on trial for crimes against “international morality and the sanctity of treatises,” but the monarch fled to the Netherlands and the Allies failed to agree on charges. As Douglas shows, the Nuremberg war crimes tribunal after World War II led to the recognition of “aggressive war” as a crime, extending international law to both external military aggression and the systematic atrocities committed by the Nazi state against its own people. Despite that success, Douglas argues that the lack of legal clarity at the tribunal over what constituted “crimes of aggression” has lingered, frustrating efforts by champions of international law to bring the perpetrators of state violence to justice.
